Xuthar opened his journal, steadied the page against the wind, and wrote only what he could bear to remember: Five stood together. Hogger fell. Then he closed the book and turned his face toward the road.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXX · The Painted Proof
pages.title: What the Gnolls Leave Behind
paragraphs: After Hogger's fall, the western edge of Elwynn refused to become peaceful merely because one feared creature was gone. Along the broken ground south of the garrison, smaller bands of Riverpaw gnolls moved among the grasses and low trees. Their voices carried over the earth in harsh bursts, then faded again into the rustle of leaves. Xuthar had imagined that the aftermath of a great struggle might grant him a quiet road. Instead it offered more work.

There was a task to be done for the watch at Westbrook, proof to gather from the creatures that had made the border uneasy. Yet the signs of their defeat were strangely difficult to come by. Three painted armbands lay among the things he had recovered; the rest remained as elusive as a name spoken into the wind. The count looked meagre against the time it had taken to reach it.

He paused beneath the thinning branches and turned one of the bands between his fingers. A strip of painted cloth was a poor measure of courage, and a poorer measure of suffering. Somewhere nearby, soldiers would know the difference between a rumour and proof. Somewhere farther west, families had learned the hard way what happened when such dangers went unanswered. Still, Xuthar wondered how much of any life could be reduced to the objects it left behind.

The road had begun to offer him other obligations. A report waited for Gryan Stoutmantle at Sentinel Hill. There was word of a simple compass hidden in an old family place, an object that meant more to its owner than its worth in coin. That small detail troubled Xuthar more deeply than he expected. He, too, carried things that were almost useless except to memory. A book of names. A broken family story. A warning he had never learned to obey.

A gnoll's distant cry broke his thoughts. Xuthar drew his robe close and looked again toward the tree line. Patience was not a hymn to suffering; sometimes wisdom meant leaving an unfinished task for another day. But the three armbands were there, and the border still held its uneasy silence. He tucked the cloth away and continued, one careful step after another.

The hours wore their way across the sky. The first three armbands had been an invitation to doubt; the fourth offered no more comfort, nor the fifth. He moved between the sparse trees and the edge of the road, nursing every remaining strength and listening for the raw cries that carried from one gnoll camp to another. The task had become less a contest of weapons than a test of whether a weary man would continue when nothing seemed to change.

By the time the last painted strip joined the others, the light had begun to soften. Xuthar spread them across a flat stone, one after another, until there were eight. None of the pieces looked important by itself. Together they meant the task was done; somewhere beyond these thickets, a patch of road might be a little safer for those who travelled it. He folded the cloth without ceremony and let his shoulders loosen at last.

He thought of the four strangers who had stood with him against Hogger. In that fight courage had moved through five bodies like a single breath. Here, in the patient work of the borderlands, he had discovered a quieter sort of courage: the refusal to turn away merely because the world offered no applause. Perhaps the ledger should hold that truth as carefully as it held any name.

The sky beyond the western trees seemed broader now. Westfall had not yet surrendered its stories, and Gryan Stoutmantle waited somewhere on the road ahead. Xuthar closed his book, gathered the eight painted bands, and turned west. The gnoll hunt was behind him. The next life to remember was waiting beyond the fields.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXXI · Beyond the Western Gate
pages.title: Where the Forest Gives Way to Gold
paragraphs: The village had been alive long before Xuthar reached its square. Around the stone road of Goldshire, travellers lingered in scattered knots, a restless assembly of robes, leather and steel. A violet glow shivered above the gathering like a fragment of twilight caught in daylight. Near the inn, familiar faces went about their ordinary business, and Marshal Dughan remained among those whose work rarely ended. Xuthar walked through the commotion without demanding that it make room for him.

He had already learned that crowds could conceal as much loneliness as a deserted road. Every traveller carried some reason for leaving or returning: a letter to deliver, an old quarrel to settle, a hunger that work might not satisfy. He wondered how many would be remembered when the square grew quiet. For a moment he thought of Carro Steelcave, his old friend, and of the roads on which their wandering lives would surely meet again. Then the movement around him thinned, and the western path called.

The way out of Goldshire entered the deep shade of Elwynn. Trees towered over the paving stones, their roots buried beneath moss and old rain. Small wooden fences guided the traveller through clearings, while shafts of pale sun lay across the road like abandoned ribbons. There were no great banners here and no one to announce the passing of a priest. Xuthar preferred it that way.

As he went, the forest seemed to close behind him. The village voices faded. He could hear his own boots again, a quiet, regular sound upon the worn stones. Once, he might have hurried in search of a destination certain to offer answers. Now he understood that the length of a road was part of its meaning. Hogger had fallen to the shared strength of five adventurers; the Riverpaw hunt had finally ended with eight painted armbands. Yet these victories had not made the world simple. They had merely allowed him to keep walking.

At last the trees opened before a stone bridge. Two carved lions watched over the crossing, and above the arch hung blue standards marked with the gold lion of Stormwind. Water moved beneath the pale masonry, carrying the reflection of a sky brighter than the forest had allowed. Xuthar stopped on the approach. A boundary drawn on a map could be crossed in a heartbeat, but the end of a familiar place asked for a longer farewell.

He looked back once. Somewhere behind the trees lay Northshire Abbey, Goldshire, the river where he had fished, the dark mines that had nearly kept him forever. He had left no monument in those places. All he carried from them were a few possessions, the weariness of experience, and the stubborn promise to remember the lives that had briefly touched his own.

Then he crossed. The stone fell away behind him, and Elwynn's green silence gave way to an immense country of gold. Westfall spread beneath the open sky: dry fields, autumn-red trees, haystacks standing like mute sentries, a weathered farmhouse, and a windmill turning far off against the haze. A cart rested by the roadside among people whose day had been shaped by labour rather than adventure.

The light made the land beautiful. It did not make it prosperous. The fields seemed to hold a tiredness that sunlight could not hide, and among the distant rows moved shapes whose purpose the priest could not yet know. He resisted the old temptation to settle the meaning of a place at first sight. A kingdom might call its harvest plentiful while the people who planted it went hungry. A traveller might mistake silence for peace because no one had asked him to listen.

Xuthar paused beside the track, turned his face into the warm wind and opened the Morvayne ledger. The pages stirred beneath his hand. He did not ask the Void what the land would become, nor did he pray for a convenient answer. Instead he wrote a new place at the head of an empty page: Westfall.

Somewhere beyond these first farms, Gryan Stoutmantle waited at Sentinel Hill. The report still rested among Xuthar's duties; no meeting had yet taken place. That was how stories truly began, he thought—not with a prophecy already fulfilled, but with a road still stretching ahead. He closed the book and stepped into the wheat-coloured afternoon.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXXII · The Weight of Wood
pages.title: The Staff and the City
paragraphs: Westfall had scarcely opened its wide, golden country to him before the road bent back toward Stormwind. Xuthar would have liked to remain among the fields, to follow the dust toward Sentinel Hill and learn what the land was asking of him. But a life travelled on foot was made of interruptions as much as destinations. There were errands to attend to in the city, small necessities that could not be soothed by watching the wheat move in the wind.

He retraced the way east. In memory, the lion-guarded bridge still held the last green light of Elwynn on one side and the dry radiance of Westfall on the other. Neither landscape had offered an answer to the sentence in the Morvayne ledger. Both had given him something more useful: a new reason to keep asking.

Stormwind received him with the restless music of a city that had never learned to be still. Footsteps and distant voices filled its streets, and each passing figure seemed to have somewhere more urgent to be. Xuthar completed what business had brought him back without feeling the need to turn every ordinary errand into a tale of heroism. A traveller who could not care for the necessities of his journey would soon find little strength left for the lives of others.

There was another change that day, a humble one to anyone accustomed to bearing arms. He learned the proper handling of a staff. It was not an incantation, not a secret of the Void, nor a revelation wrested from some hidden page. It was the patient understanding that a length of wood could become more than an awkward weight in the hands: a way to keep one's balance, to stand one's ground, to meet danger without surrendering to panic.

A new staff had come into his possession. Xuthar examined it without imagining that its worth lay in an ancient name or a destiny etched upon its surface. For now it was simply new to him. He felt its unfamiliar promise, and the slight embarrassment of learning a skill that others seemed to take for granted. There was comfort in beginning again, even after the tenth threshold of his travels.

The tailor's shop was fuller than Xuthar had expected. Bolts of coloured cloth crowded the shelves; jars of dye and lengths of thread stood between the counter and the stair. A dozen voices overlapped in the warm room. Travellers in fine robes stood shoulder to shoulder with apprentices whose sleeves still bore the uneven signs of their first repairs. For once, a priest who had faced gnolls on the open road could scarcely find a clear path to a merchant.

Antonio Bolero stood among his patterns, Alexandra among the necessary supplies, and Lawrence Schneider near the stair. Giorgio Bolero, the more accomplished artisan, could be seen beyond the bustle. Xuthar waited. Not because a stern rule required it—any traveller might have pressed forward and been served—but because he had no desire to mistake his own errands for the most important business in the room.

He watched the hands around him: hands used to war trying to learn a gentler craft, careful fingers choosing thread, tired shoulders carrying rolled fabric. The city was always full of grand declarations about duty and victory, yet here survival looked like a seam that held, a hem that did not fray, a coat made warm enough for the next cold road. He found himself smiling faintly. Perhaps patience, too, was a kind of tailoring: it gave the rough hours a shape they could bear.

The first bags he completed were modest things, stitched together by hands that had grown more accustomed to the weight of a staff than the resistance of a needle. Their cloth would never be mistaken for a master artisan's work, but Xuthar turned them over with quiet satisfaction. He had made room where there had been none. A traveller carried so many small necessities—thread, food, fragments of old paper, things kept for reasons too private to explain. Now they need not all compete for the same narrow space.

It was a strange kind of victory, and a useful one. Not every problem demanded prayer or the Shadow. Sometimes the answer was simply a stronger seam and a little patience. Xuthar drew the bag's mouth closed and imagined the road ahead less burdened by what he had to leave behind.

The Light had once taught him that power should be used in service. The Shadow had taught him how carefully power must be questioned. This new discipline asked something quieter: hold what you carry without allowing it to decide who you are. A staff was neither mercy nor cruelty. The hands guiding it would have to choose.

In the end, the ledger remained his more troublesome possession. Its old line still waited beneath the pages: The last witness must not remember. He had not deciphered it in Stormwind. No errand had brought him closer to an explanation. Yet there were now more names, more roads and another small lesson to record beside it.

Beyond the walls lay Westfall, where golden fields and difficult stories waited for his return. Gryan Stoutmantle still belonged to the road ahead. Xuthar looked once toward the city's way out, the new staff among his travelling belongings, and found that he was in no hurry to call a detour a failure. Sometimes the journey changed a man most when he briefly walked the wrong direction.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXXIII · The Watchers in the Wheat
pages.title: Where the Harvest Stood Guard
paragraphs: The road to Westfall welcomed Xuthar a second time without ceremony. Behind him lay the clamour of Stormwind and the close warmth of the tailor's shop; ahead, the country unfolded in broad, gold-coloured furrows beneath a pale sky. He had returned with a staff he was only beginning to know and bags sewn by his own hands. They were not the possessions of a great hero, but they were enough for a man determined to make his way.

Near the road a wagon had become a small monument to plans gone wrong. Its owners, Farmer Furlbrow and his wife Verna, spoke of a home the surrounding troubles had made unsafe. They had tried to leave, yet the road had held them still. Xuthar listened to the worried voices and saw in their halted journey something he knew too well: the peculiar cruelty of a world that could take away a person's home before granting them anywhere else to belong.

Verna Furlbrow's recipe was a modest inheritance of another kind. She wanted it carried to Salma Saldean, so that something warm and familiar might outlive the farm she was leaving behind. It was only a way of making stew, yet Xuthar received the folded instructions with the solemnity he might have given a page rescued from a burning library. He had learned that memory sometimes survived most faithfully in the ordinary things people passed from hand to hand.

The farmer's request was harder to hear. He had left a pocket watch in a wardrobe at the old farmhouse to the west, among the pumpkins and the men who had driven them away. It had been a wedding gift from Verna's father. The priest could imagine a watch ticking through years of small shared moments, seasons measured not in wars or kings but in suppers, harvests and mornings beside the same familiar face. To lose it would be to lose a little piece of the life the couple had already been forced to surrender.

He could promise only to try. The recipe had not yet reached Salma, and the watch was still somewhere in the unsafe farmhouse. Beyond the wagon, the road toward Sentinel Hill remained unfinished too. Xuthar set these obligations carefully beside the others he carried. He had come west in search of the stories of a troubled land; already that land had given him two names and two fragile ways of remembering.

The first fields seemed almost impossibly beautiful. Rows of earth ran across the hills in clean dark lines, and between them lay pumpkins in hundreds, their round orange bodies catching the afternoon light. A barn rose beyond the far rows, its timbers worn and weathered, with a smaller house close by. Autumn had set the trees aflame with red and copper. In another land, the same sight might have promised a generous harvest and a peaceful winter.

Something moved among the pumpkins. At first Xuthar took the shapes for labourers bent over their work. Then one rose to its full height, all rough limbs, heavy frame and movements too abrupt to belong to any farmer. Others stood across the fields. These were the Harvest Watchers, guardians of a crop that no longer seemed entirely under human care.

Their very name unsettled him. A watcher should protect. A harvest should feed. But words were only promises, and the world was full of promises twisted out of recognition. From the edge of a furrow Xuthar counted the hulking figures and felt the familiar counsel of caution return. He had survived the gnolls not because he believed himself invincible, but because he had learned to recognize danger before it found its way to him.

Travellers were scattered through the farm. Some passed near the standing creatures, others hurried from one line of pumpkins to another, and the whole field seemed to shift between work and conflict. Xuthar watched without pretending to know the purpose of every stranger. Nor did he mistake the sight of a dangerous machine for a battle that had already been won.

He rested one hand upon his new staff. The wood was still strange against his palm, its balance different from the implements he had carried before. The new bags at his side gave him a little more space for the road, yet no amount of empty space could carry certainty. Westfall had already begun to teach him that the most ordinary landscapes could hide the hardest questions.

He thought of the faces in Stormwind's crowded tailoring shop. There, people had struggled for thread and cloth, trying to mend what had worn thin. Here, in the very fields that might have clothed or fed them, the harvest had acquired iron guardians. The contrast struck him more deeply than any threat of claws or teeth. What had happened to a kingdom, he wondered, when a field needed watchers and its people still looked hungry?

The priest lowered his gaze to the dark earth between the rows. He could follow the road onward toward Sentinel Hill, where Gryan Stoutmantle and the unfinished report waited, or linger here until the story of these fields became clearer. He chose not to force an answer. The wind ran through the pumpkins, the watchers stirred in the distance, and the last witness listened.

That evening, whatever the road might bring, one image would remain: a small figure in red and dark cloth standing among immense furrows, looking toward an autumn farm that seemed to hold both abundance and ruin in the same breath. In Westfall, even the harvest had a shadow.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXXIV · A Harvest Without Plenty
pages.title: The Hunger Beneath the Gold
paragraphs: The fields of Westfall did not empty when Xuthar looked away from the Harvest Watchers. They continued their slow, uneasy passage between the furrows as though the ground had given them orders no living farmer could rescind. He found himself measuring each movement, and the distance between one heavy frame and the next. Somewhere, men had decided that twenty of these walking guardians ought to be brought down. Xuthar had not yet struck the first.

It seemed a cruel joke that a land so thick with crops should speak so insistently of hunger. Hay stood in dry stacks; pumpkins lay against the earth like glowing embers; the barns rose broad and old beneath the autumn light. Yet the people who lived here had their thoughts fixed on food, debts and the things they had lost. The priest had seen hunger before, but here it wore the face of abundance.

Verna Furlbrow's recipe had begun as a small plea to carry something familiar onward. Now it had become another set of needs, scattered across fields, marshes and roadside paths. There were vegetables among his gathered provisions, round green okra collected one by one until that part of the task was satisfied. But the stew could not yet be made. A little tough meat and the first of the boars' spoils were not enough; what he sought from the murlocs remained wholly beyond his reach.

The boars were stubborn creatures, hard to bring down and harder still to search through when the blood cooled. Twice he had recovered what was needed for a liver pie, and six times more fortune would have to favour him before that errand could be called finished. The work was neither glorious nor clean. There were no songs for a traveller counting the contents of a bag in the dust. He was almost grateful for that. Glory had a habit of hiding the cost of things.

He thought of the crowded tailor's shop in Stormwind, the weight of his new staff and the bags he had sewn there. The extra space mattered now. One bag held food gathered for another household; another made room for the odds and ends of a road whose purpose kept shifting. A needle and a length of thread had done something no dramatic incantation could do: allowed him to carry more of other people's troubles without abandoning his own.

Beyond the farm, the old Furlbrow watch still waited to be recovered. Farther on, Gryan Stoutmantle remained an unmet obligation at Sentinel Hill. Xuthar could have sworn that every road in Westfall ended in someone asking for help, but he did not resent the asking. The terrible thing would be a place in which nobody expected help to come.

A gust of wind drew pale dust across the rows. The Harvest Watchers turned slowly in the fading brightness, their harsh shapes briefly softened by the haze. Xuthar kept his distance. He had seen one of them close enough to understand how much stronger it was than he, and caution did not become cowardice simply because the task ahead was large.

He opened the Morvayne ledger beneath the branches of a red-leafed tree. The next lines were plain: a field guarded by machines, a farmer's keepsake still lost, an unfinished stew, a report still to be made. He had begun this journey searching for the meaning of memory; Westfall was teaching him something more immediate. A memory could not feed a hungry child. But remembering who was hungry might be the first reason to act.

Above the fields the evening sky was the colour of old paper. Xuthar shut the ledger and listened to the wind moving across the crops. The harvest looked golden from a distance. Closer, it was a thousand unfinished duties. He stepped back onto the path, the quiet witness to a country that could produce so much and still leave its people wanting.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXXV · The Eleventh Threshold
pages.title: The Weight of Another Dawn
paragraphs: By the time the shadows lengthened across the fields of Westfall, Xuthar had begun to understand that the land was not quiet at all. Its silence was layered with smaller sounds: wind dragging through stubble, the dull groan of timber beyond a barn, the uneven tread of travellers who kept one eye upon the road and the other upon the things that wandered through the harvest. Once he would have mistaken the golden distance for peace. Now he knew better.

He had spent the day moving between obligations that seemed too ordinary to belong in any tale worth remembering. A recipe to carry. An heirloom to recover. Food gathered in small, insufficient portions. A grim count of harvest machines that had yet to be confronted. None of it resembled the stories told beneath the high roofs of Stormwind, where victory was a clean word and suffering happened conveniently far from the speaker.

The Furlbrows had taught him otherwise. Their halted wagon stood in his thoughts long after he left it behind, its burden of simple possessions more eloquent than a soldier's speech. He imagined a house stripped of its familiar hours: the sound of a spoon against a bowl, the creak of a chair, the ordinary act of checking the time. The little watch still lay beyond his reach, and he found its absence harder to forget than any treasure he had ever coveted.

A breeze rose from the furrows and touched the new staff in his hand. He was still learning its weight. The wood did not answer the questions that crowded his mind, nor did it steady itself when he gripped it poorly. It merely waited for him to learn. He had known teachers who spoke of power as though it were a possession. This quiet implement offered a less flattering lesson: strength was an agreement between patience and practice, renewed each time the road became difficult.

The bags he had sewn in Stormwind hung at his side. Their seams were modest, their usefulness undeniable. As Xuthar shifted the weight of the gathered provisions, he remembered the crowded tailor's shop, the bolts of cloth, the people pressing toward the counter. He had not gone there seeking a revelation. Yet the hours spent with needle and thread had given him something that prayer alone could not: room to carry the necessities of other people's lives.

His progress had been like that, he realized. Not a sudden transformation, but a series of almost invisible concessions to the world. He had learned to rest when he was wounded, to accept the aid of strangers against Hogger, to remain in the gnolls' country long after he wanted to leave, and to cross a bridge even when the road on the far side frightened him. Each small act had altered the next. He could no longer pretend to be quite the man who had set out from Northshire.

It was here, amid the stubborn gold of the harvest, that he felt another threshold pass beneath his feet. There was no procession, no bell from a distant abbey, no voice naming the change. The same tired boots stood in the same dusty soil. And yet something in the way he looked upon the world had shifted. What once seemed a landscape full of tasks had become a country full of people whose sorrows had waited for someone to notice them.

He sat for a little while beside the road, where the shade of an autumn tree had crept across the stones. He opened the Morvayne ledger, turning slowly past names that had meant nothing to him before the journey began. Some belonged to people he had helped. Others were merely people he had seen and wished, afterward, that he had known better. Each page gave him a reason to believe that the book was growing into something his family had never intended.

Near the centre lay the old warning, as sharp as ever: The last witness must not remember. Xuthar traced the words without touching the ink. He had once feared that the sentence foretold a punishment. Now he wondered whether it was an instruction left by someone who feared what remembering might expose. The difference unsettled him. A threat could be faced. A truth, once known, might demand that he become someone else.

For a moment he thought of Carro Steelcave. Their paths were not joined tonight, but the thought of his old friend reminded him that a life was not only the battles one survived alone. Somewhere along the roads ahead they would meet again, and Xuthar hoped to have more to offer than stories of danger. Perhaps he could tell Carro about the watch he meant to find, the people whose dinner depended on an unfinished recipe, and a country that had forgotten how to feed those who worked its fields.

The sun lowered. In the distance a Harvest Watcher turned between the pumpkins, heavy and tireless, while travellers moved along the far road. The twenty machines he had been asked to destroy were still an untouched burden, just as Gryan Stoutmantle's report remained unspoken. There was no shame in unfinished work, he told himself, provided it was not forgotten. Tomorrow—or another day, when the road allowed—it would still be there.

Xuthar shut the ledger and rose. He had crossed no visible boundary, yet he felt the distance he had travelled more keenly than the ache in his legs. Beneath the fading light, Westfall was still beautiful and still wounded. The priest settled his staff against the stones and began to walk again, neither saved by the Light nor surrendered to the Shadow, but willing to witness what came next.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXXVI · The Hearthward Road
pages.title: The Weight of What Remains
paragraphs: By late afternoon the golden fields had ceased to look like a promise. Westfall still wore the same beautiful light, the same rust-red trees and orderly furrows; but Xuthar had spent too long among them to mistake their colour for kindness. Dust gathered in the folds of his robe. His hands were sore, and every mile seemed to add another small burden to a day already heavy with them.

He had made progress, and that was almost the worst of it. There was enough tough meat for the stew, enough of the boars' snouts, and every last piece of okra that the recipe demanded. Two murloc eyes had joined the provisions as well. But not the third. A single missing thing stood between him and a meal someone else might finally prepare, and the stubborn absence of it grew in his thoughts until it seemed larger than the fields themselves.

Another household wanted livers for a pie, and that errand had scarcely begun to yield what it required. The Furlbrows' wedding watch remained lost in their abandoned farmhouse. The Harvest Watchers moved among the pumpkins without one of their number having fallen to him. Even Gryan Stoutmantle was still a name waiting at the end of an untravelled stretch of road. The priest looked from one obligation to another and wondered how a man was meant to measure the good he had done when the unfinished work always seemed to multiply.

His new bags had been sewn with such satisfaction in Stormwind. Now their seams carried everything they could reasonably hold, and the irony nearly made him laugh. He had spent precious time learning to make space, only to discover that the world could fill it faster than any needle moved through cloth. An odd assortment of provisions pressed against the pages and small tools he guarded so carefully. He could no longer find what he needed without first lifting half the contents of his journey into the daylight.

The unfamiliar staff rested against his shoulder. He had learned to hold it, but there were moments when he still felt how little he knew. A wand would serve him better in certain dangers, he thought; perhaps one could be found when next he reached Stormwind. There were also matters of tailoring and enchanting to put in order, supplies to examine and the ordinary business of a traveller who expected to return to hostile roads. He had begun to understand that preparation was not the opposite of bravery. Sometimes it was the only honest form bravery could take.

He stopped where the path rose slightly above the fields. Wind slid through the furrows, setting the dry stalks whispering against one another. The autumn sky was wide and indifferent. Xuthar thought of pressing onward, of finding one more murloc, searching one more ruined room, doing something—anything—that might let him call the day complete. But his tiredness had become a warning he could no longer dismiss.

There were defeats that left no wound. They arrived as small mistakes made by exhausted hands, a wrong turning taken after dusk, a creature approached too closely because one had lost the patience to watch. Xuthar had already learned that lesson in the mines of Elwynn, and he had no wish to learn it again merely to satisfy his pride. He took the Hearthstone from his belongings. In his palm its familiar shape felt impossibly ordinary for an object capable of folding the road back upon itself.

For a moment he held it without moving. Westfall remained before him: the farms, the needy families, the mechanical sentries and the broken promises beneath a magnificent harvest. Leaving did not erase them. Yet the thought of walking away while so many were still waiting stung more sharply than the ache in his feet. He had spent his life trying to make memory into a duty; now he discovered how easily duty could become a chain.

He closed his eyes and let the stone answer. The hard lines of the fields dissolved into a gathering glow. Wind, dust and the distant cries of the farmland seemed to fall away together, as though the world had turned a page too quickly for him to read the end of it. When the light released him, the familiar air of Goldshire surrounded him once more.

There was comfort in recognising a place without having to search for it. Goldshire was no grand sanctuary, only a village where boots wore the paving stones smooth and travellers came and went beneath the patient shadows of Elwynn. Yet the road there did not demand an answer from him at every step. He stood for a while, carrying the weight of provisions and unfinished promises, and allowed himself the simple relief of having returned.

Stormwind lay farther on. There he meant to empty his crowded bags, attend to the neglected work of his professions, and find a wand worthy of the dangerous roads ahead. Before any of that, he needed rest. None of these things had yet been accomplished. For once, Xuthar was willing to let tomorrow remain unwritten.

He opened the Morvayne ledger and considered the warning that had survived within it for so long: The last witness must not remember. Today memory had offered no answers; it had offered only the faces of people still waiting for help. Perhaps that was why the words troubled him. He could forget his own exhaustion more easily than he could forget Verna's recipe or the absent watch that had once measured the hours of a marriage.

At last he made a smaller entry on an otherwise empty page. Not a tally of victories, nor a list of things carried home. He wrote that the road could be left unfinished without being abandoned. Then he shut the book, adjusted the heavy straps of his bags, and turned toward the way to Stormwind. Beyond the trees, Westfall would go on waiting. So would he, until he had the strength to return.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXXVII · The Quiet Art of Enchantment
pages.title: What the Ordinary Things Remember
paragraphs: The road back from Westfall had taken Xuthar away from the golden fields, but it had not loosened their hold upon him. Even after the familiar warmth of Goldshire returned, he found the shapes of the Harvest Watchers moving behind his eyes. They were guardians that had forgotten what it meant to guard; the people around them were hungry in a country that should have fed them. He had carried those contradictions home along with the unfinished stew and the small, stubborn weight of a farmer's lost watch.

Rest had not come easily. There were provisions to sort, scraps of cloth to fold and small things to put in order before the next stretch of road. The bags he had made with his own hands stood beside him, their seams holding firm beneath their burden. Not long ago he had considered needlework an unlikely occupation for a priest of the Shadow. Now it seemed almost necessary. The world was forever coming apart in little places, and he had learned to mend at least a few of them.

Enchanting required a different kind of patience. Cloth answered the needle in a way he could see; the subtler work asked him to trust what remained invisible, to study how power settled into ordinary matter without allowing his thoughts to wander toward grander promises. He had learned to listen for the small resistance of a thing, to recognize when the work had taken hold and when it needed to be begun again.

In the abbey at Northshire, he had been taught to distinguish the sacred from the profane. The Light had spoken through rituals and reassuring certainties, while the Shadow arrived with questions that seemed to sharpen the longer he considered them. Enchanting belonged neatly to neither. It asked for attention, not allegiance. It cared little for the name a man gave his power, only for the discipline with which he used it.

That discovery comforted him more than he expected. He had spent so long wondering whether the Void would change him beyond recognition that he sometimes forgot the simpler question of what he wished to change in the world. A stronger thread. A traveller better prepared for the road. Some small help offered without a witness to praise it. Not everything needed to become a test of the soul.

He returned to the practice again and again, allowing each attempt to teach him a little more. The work did not offer the sudden thrill of a hard-won battle. Its victories were quieter, and because of that perhaps harder to recognise. At last the elementary discipline that had once stood before him like an unfinished lesson was complete. One obligation, at least, could be set down without regret.

Xuthar sat with his hands resting upon his knees. For a moment he imagined the unfinished page in the Morvayne ledger filling itself with the names of everything he had not managed: the final murloc eye, the livers still to gather, the pocket watch, the report waiting at Sentinel Hill. The list was long enough that he could almost feel it pressing against the covers. But the new skill did not belong among those absences. It was a reminder that persistence could leave something lasting behind.

His thoughts turned to Carro Steelcave, whose friendship had survived stretches of road too long for easy meetings. Carro would probably have laughed at the sight of him so solemn over a little craftwork. Xuthar could almost hear the laughter, and found himself smiling. He hoped that when they met again he could tell his friend about something other than danger: the unfamiliar pleasure of becoming useful in ways he had never imagined.

Still, he would not mistake preparation for arrival. The wand he hoped to obtain remained ahead, as did the errands of tailoring and the return to Westfall. No teacher had dismissed the needs of Gryan Stoutmantle, nor had any charm conjured the missing ingredient for Salma's stew. Enchanting had taught him how to bring care to an object; it could not choose whom he should care for.

He opened the Morvayne ledger where the old warning waited beneath the ink: The last witness must not remember. Perhaps that command had been meant to silence a dangerous truth. Perhaps it was simply a cruelty left by frightened people. Tonight Xuthar set another thought beside it: memory was not only the keeping of wounds. Sometimes it was the keeping of a lesson, so that the hands which had once failed might one day know how to help.

He shut the book gently. Beyond his brief shelter the kingdom remained restless, and Westfall waited with its wheat-coloured fields and unanswered pleas. The priest had not finished his journey. He had only learned one more way to carry its weight.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXXVIII · Beneath the Eastern Boughs
pages.title: The Wood That Kept Its Secrets
paragraphs: The roads of Elwynn had begun to feel familiar, but familiarity was not the same as knowing. Xuthar had returned to Goldshire by the grace of a Hearthstone, with the dust of Westfall still clinging to his clothes and the names of its hungry families lingering at the edges of his thoughts. Now, rather than turn again toward the golden fields, he followed the forest east. There were lives here too, lives whose troubles had not yet found their way into the Morvayne ledger.

The change came slowly. The wide land narrowed beneath older branches, and the smell of dry wheat gave way to damp bark and the clean, bitter scent of cut timber. Somewhere beyond the trees lay the work of Eastvale's loggers. A kingdom built its towers and repaired its roofs from wood such as this, yet the men who felled the trees seldom received a line in any chronicle. Xuthar wondered how much of Stormwind rested on shoulders history would never name.

He passed through a country of uneven tracks, deep roots and shafts of pale light. The new staff rested more naturally in his hand than it had on the day he learned to wield it. Beneath his robes the weight of his carefully sewn bags had changed too. Westfall had filled them with the makings of a humble meal, and at last every ingredient of Salma's stew was accounted for. The food was ready to be carried back, though the promise to deliver it was not yet fulfilled.

It should have made him feel triumphant. Instead he remembered how easy it was to mistake possessing something for having finished the work it demanded. The last murloc eye could be counted beside the others, but the people of Westfall would not eat a meal because he counted well. He would have to return. The unfinished pie, the wedding watch and the unspoken report to Gryan Stoutmantle waited on the same road.

The forest ahead offered its own obligations. A man named Rolf was missing, and somewhere near a murloc village there might be signs of what had happened to him. No voice had told Xuthar the answer. He knew only the particular dread of being sent to look for a man when others had already begun to fear that they were searching for the dead. The priest kept the name close in his thoughts without allowing himself to turn suspicion into certainty.

There were other dangers along the frontier. Prowlers haunted the undergrowth, and young bears wandered close enough to trouble those who worked among the trees. The count of beasts he had been asked to confront still stood untouched. Xuthar looked into the darker spaces between the trunks and chose his steps with care. Hunting had taught him patience, but he had never believed that every creature in a forest was his enemy simply because a frightened settlement had given it a number.

The affairs of the loggers were humbler and, in a way, more revealing. An axe, a saw and a toolbox had been lost to the water. Mining tools were wanted elsewhere. Bundles of wood needed gathering. To a distant lord these might have seemed small inconveniences. To men whose living depended upon their hands, a missing tool could mean a day's wages lost, a roof left unfinished, or a fire gone cold.

He had two red linen bandanas among the things collected along his journey. The remaining cloth was still unaccounted for, just as the stranded tools and stacked timber were. Xuthar resisted the desire to make a neat list of victories. What he carried was evidence of beginnings, not endings. The longer he walked, the more he suspected that the world was made mostly of beginnings that nobody ever thought to celebrate.

In the quiet between birdsong and the distant labour of the woods, he remembered the lessons of enchanting. Power did not always announce itself with thunder or flame; sometimes it required a steady hand and a willingness to repeat a small action until it was done properly. He could see the same truth in the forest. A road existed because someone cleared it. A bridge held because someone tightened its beams. Even a stranger's safety might depend upon a person who never learned his name.

He paused where the path curved away through the trees, the eastern woods gathering in layers ahead of him. For a moment the warning in his family's ledger seemed to rise from memory as if spoken aloud: The last witness must not remember. He had once imagined the words as a curse. In Westfall they had sounded like a threat. Here, among the work of people who might leave no written trace, they felt like an accusation.

If no one remembered the logger who lost his tools, the woman waiting for stew, the farmer's wedding watch, or Rolf whose fate remained hidden, then what difference was there between a kingdom and a forest that swallowed its own paths? Xuthar touched the leather cover of the ledger. He had no answer, and he had only recently learned to stop being ashamed of that.

The shadows lengthened under the boughs. He moved east again, neither certain of what he would find nor willing to invent the end of a stranger's story. Westfall waited behind him; the woods of Elwynn waited ahead. For the moment, that was enough. The road did not ask him to be a hero. It asked him to keep walking, to look closely, and to remember the names he was about to learn.

pages.chapter: Chapter XXXIX · Work Among the Trees
pages.title: The Price of a Safer Road
paragraphs: The eastern forest had a different kind of silence from Westfall. The golden fields spoke in wind and dry grass; the woods near Eastvale answered with the creak of branches and the distant blows of axes. Each sound travelled strangely beneath the canopy, close one moment and impossibly far away the next. Xuthar walked where carts had pressed ruts into the earth, following the uncertain border between a place of labour and a place that still belonged to the wild.

He had come looking for small duties to ease the weight of the unfinished work behind him. The forest did not offer such comfort. Men who had to move between the trees feared the prowlers hidden in the brush and the young bears that wandered too close to their paths. Xuthar had never liked the ease with which fear became an order to kill. Yet he could not dismiss the fear of people whose lives depended on crossing those same paths every morning.

The work was neither swift nor clean. He learned to read the movement of leaves that had no wind behind them, and to recognise when an animal was ready to spring. He held his staff more surely than before, but it was his caution that kept him alive. When the last of the creatures threatening the frontier had fallen, the paths felt no less wild. They were simply a little safer for those who had to use them.

For a time he stood beneath the trees without moving. The dead had not become less real because they wore fur rather than mail. He remembered the solemn assurances of priests who spoke as though every necessary act were therefore an easy one. Xuthar could not share their certainty. If danger had been kept from the loggers, that was something worth doing. It did not require him to rejoice.

Elsewhere the work was quieter. Four missing mining tools had to be gathered, their usefulness as plain as their rough handles. He imagined the people who would take them up again: workers too tired to think of destiny, who needed a good piece of steel more urgently than they needed a blessing. The tools seemed heavy with the ordinary authority of labour. He handled them carefully.

The red linen bandanas told another story. He had come upon the first two earlier in his wanderings; now the remainder of the required cloth was accounted for. Their colour recalled the darker stains he had seen along the roads of Elwynn. He folded the fabric with a strange unease, wondering how easily a piece of common clothing could become a sign of allegiance, fear or violence, depending upon whose hands had held it.

Three duties had reached the point where he could return and tell their petitioners that the work was done. He had not yet made those returns. Xuthar had learned the difference between carrying proof and delivering it, between a promise fulfilled in the forest and one acknowledged by the people who had made it. His bags held more than objects now. They held unfinished conversations.

There was still no trace of Rolf's fate. Somewhere near the murlocs, a missing man's story waited behind reeds and water, and the priest refused to decide its ending without seeing what the river had kept. An axe, a saw and a toolbox still lay beyond his reach, swallowed by the current or hidden along its banks. Bundles of wood remained to be collected. Each errand drew him toward a different part of the same troubled country.

And to the west, another waiting list crossed his mind: Salma's stew, its ingredients finally gathered but not yet delivered; the farmer's pocket watch; Gryan Stoutmantle on Sentinel Hill; the restless machinery among the pumpkins. He was beginning to understand that a journey did not move neatly from one victory to the next. More often it moved through obligations that overlapped, like the branches above him, until it was impossible to say where one ended and another began.

The Morvayne ledger rested against his side, bound in worn leather and stubborn questions. The last witness must not remember. He thought of the animals left in the undergrowth, the labourers waiting for their steel, the red cloth gathered from the forest, and the man named Rolf whose absence had become an errand. If remembering was a danger, perhaps it was because memory refused to make the world simpler than it was.

He turned back toward the worn path, where a gap in the canopy allowed a pale strip of evening sky to show through. He had made the road safer. He had recovered what had been sought. Yet the eastern woods still held a missing man, lost tools and timber waiting to be carried home. Xuthar walked on, his hands tired, his purpose steadier. The forest had not given him an ending. It had given him reasons to return.

pages.chapter: Epilogue · The Unwritten Road
pages.title: What the Next Dawn May Bring
paragraphs: At the edge of the latest page, the ink thinned. Xuthar sat with the ledger open, his belongings close at hand, listening to distant footsteps and the restless sounds of a world that had never waited for any one man.

Somewhere beyond Elwynn a western road turned toward unfamiliar fields. In the east, old mines held their darkness. And scattered between those distant places were people who had yet to know his name, though one day their stories might be written beside his.
He did not call the empty pages a failure. A life was not complete because it had been neatly described. It was complete only when its last road had truly ended, and he had not reached that road.
Xuthar closed the book gently. The last witness was still alive. That was enough to promise another chapter.

pages.chapter: Front matter
pages.title: For the ones who will follow
paragraphs: Some maps are made to claim land. The best ones are made so another traveller can find the way home.

Thorgar Ironbeard has not yet begun his journey in Forever. What follows is the personal fiction that will travel in his pack when his time arrives. His real achievements, companions and routes are still unwritten.

pages.chapter: Chapter I · Ironforge
pages.title: Brass, ink and stubbornness
paragraphs: Thorgar's childhood smelled of metal polish, fresh paper and the sharp warmth of a forge. His family repaired instruments for people who left Ironforge with hopes too large for their pockets. He learned to measure twice, not because his father feared mistakes, but because strangers might trust the work.
His mother preserved ledgers and maps with a severity the boy understood only years later. Every corrected distance meant a stranger might arrive before nightfall.
The mountain raised him, but every departing caravan taught him that the world had more corners than a well-made map could contain.
pages.caption: Illustrative Ironforge archive.

pages.chapter: Chapter II · The survey
pages.title: Six stones, seven signatures
paragraphs: In an old drawer he found a survey that listed six stone cairns and carried seven names. The last signature had been scraped away. Someone had written a warning on the edge: Do not count the seventh.

Thorgar asked for an explanation and was given three different stories. His father called the document damaged; an older relative said the expedition had ended safely. Nobody seemed eager to compare their memories.
He took the family's brass compass to his workbench. Its needle would not settle where the others did. He cleaned it, checked it, and refused to call it enchanted merely because it was inconvenient.
pages.caption: Atmospheric road illustration · Fictional survey.

pages.chapter: Prologue · The Seventh Cairn
pages.title: Where the seventh stone should be
paragraphs: There are things a mountain keeps better than a man: cold, silence, and the weight of a promise made too long ago.

Six cairns on the route. Seven signatures beneath. One scratched away until the paper nearly broke. My father saw me count them, set down his hammer, and said some trails were best left to the weather.
Perhaps the compass is broken. Perhaps my pride is. I have packed my rifle and enough supplies for a poor start; I will trust neither a map nor a rumor until the ground has had its say.
For now I shall count seven stones, though I have only ever seen six.

pages.chapter: Reserved
pages.title: A road not yet walked
paragraphs: The first real chapter will begin when Thorgar is actually played. Until then, his route, pet, friends, profession progress and choices remain unknown.
Xuthar Morvayne remains the main character whose Chronicle will grow first.

pages.chapter: Front matter
pages.title: To everything that must change
paragraphs: A place can be loved without being possessed. A song can be remembered without being forced to return.
Aelyndra's life in Forever remains ahead of her. Her faction, journeys and discoveries are not decided in these pages. They belong to future play, not the author's convenience.

pages.chapter: Chapter I · Above the clouds
pages.title: The garden on Zephras Isle
paragraphs: The gardens of Zephras Isle demanded gentle hands. Aelyndra grew among terraces where plants leaned toward the sun and the wind could interrupt the most careful work. Her mother taught her to bind young stems without constricting them.
She was fascinated less by the breadth of the sky than by the lives that persisted beneath it. A seed that survived a storm seemed as extraordinary as any ancestral tale.
When her people argued about their future, Aelyndra tried to hear what was being said beneath the anger: the fear of losing a home, and the fear of never being allowed to leave it.

pages.chapter: Chapter II · The still morning
pages.title: The fifth leaf
paragraphs: A silver chime of five leaves hung outside the family dwelling. Its notes had accompanied ordinary mornings for as long as Aelyndra remembered. One day all the plants moved in the breeze, but the chime made no sound.
She examined the hinges and cords. Nothing seemed broken. She could not prove the object meant anything beyond its own silence.
That evening she wrapped it in cloth. The island had greater troubles than an heirloom, but she suspected people first learned to recognize loss through the smallest absences.
pages.caption: Atmospheric archive illustration · Fictional family chime.

pages.chapter: Prologue · The Silent Chime
pages.title: The hour of still air
paragraphs: Some mornings the terraces sang before the sun reached them. The wind moved through chimes, leaves and narrow spaces between stone. Every sound seemed to be its own language.

Mother told me I had confused listening with naming. A thing did not become mine because I could describe it. Then the silver chime fell silent, and I understood how quickly affection can become a demand.
I have folded away my herbs and wrapped the five leaves in cloth. Soon I shall travel into a world whose winds do not know my name. I hope I will be wise enough not to demand that they learn it.
If the song returns, I would like to hear it without mistaking it for a command.

pages.chapter: Reserved
pages.title: The world beneath the clouds
paragraphs: Aelyndra's actual faction, adventures, encounters and skills will appear only once you play her in Forever.
Her personal lore is prepared, but Xuthar's chronicle comes first.
